item.title: Characterization of recombinase-based genetic parts and circuits using nanopore sequencing.
item.abstract: Recombinases are versatile enzymes able to perform the precise insertion, deletion, and rearrangement of DNA and can act as a foundation for programmable genetic logic and memory. Crucial for their use are accurate measurements of function. However, these are often laborious, time-consuming, and costly to collect. To address this, we develop a semi-automated workflow that combines low-cost liquid handling robotics, multiplexed long-read nanopore sequencing, and a supporting computational analysis tool to enable the high-throughput and detailed characterization of recombinase parts and circuits when used in a variety of contexts and organisms. Our approach overcomes the limitations of typically used fluorescence-based assays and is able to monitor temporal dynamics, observe structural changes at nucleotide resolution, and unravel the internal workings of complex multi-state circuits. The ability to scale up and automate genetic circuit characterization is an essential step towards more rigorous biological metrology that can support the construction of predictive models for efficiently engineering biology.

item.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
item.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.
item.authors: Lusi, Moncayo von Hase, Model, et al.

item.title: Efficient genome editing in ASC-derived porcine lung organoids via GFP-guided enrichment.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adult stem cell-derived organoids are invaluable tools for disease modeling and translational medicine owing to their tissue-specific correspondence. However, their complex three-dimensional structure and low genome-editing efficiency have posed significant challenges for functional genetic studies. To address these limitations, this study aimed to establish porcine lung organoid (PLOs) and to develop a robust, high-efficiency genome-editing platform by leveraging the high physiological and anatomical similarity between pigs and humans.
METHODS: PLOs were derived from lung tissues and characterized by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry analysis. To enhance genome-editing efficiency using CRISPR/Cas9 and prime editing, a GFP-guided enrichment strategy was used by co-targeting a GFP transgene and endogenous loci, followed by the selection of GFP-negative organoids. Clonal expansion from single organoids was performed to generate genetically homogenous lines. Genetic modifications were validated through cDNA sequencing and western blot analysis. Structural integrity was assessed using AlphaFold2 modeling, and functional changes were evaluated using the forskolin-induced swelling assay.
RESULTS: The established PLOs exhibited sustained self-renewal capacity and expression of surfactant protein C alongside both proximal epithelial and mesenchymal markers, reflecting a composite lung organoid identity. GFP-guided enrichment significantly enriched edited cells; the mutation ratio in the GFP-negative group was significantly higher than that in the GFP-positive group. This system successfully generated fully gene-edited clones with high genetic homogeneity, and effectively enriched for precisely edited organoids, even when applying complex modalities such as prime editing.
CONCLUSIONS: The PLOs and genome-editing platform developed in this study provide a powerful resource for translational medicine. By enabling precise genetic manipulation in a model that closely mimics human lung physiology, this system offers an essential platform for recapitulating human lung pathologies, studying zoonotic infectious diseases, and validating the efficacy of gene therapies.

item.title: Optical Control of Therapeutic Synthetic Cells: Controlling Biomolecule Synthesis, Activation, and Communication.
item.abstract: Synthetic cells are emerging as promising platforms that combine cell-free biomolecule synthesis with the programmability of bottom-up engineered compartments. By decoupling biomolecule production from cellular growth and evolutionary constraints, synthetic cells enable the controlled generation of proteins, nucleic acids, peptides, and signaling molecules within defined artificial environments. However, many envisioned biomedical applications require precise regulation over biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport, release, and communication. In this Review, we examine how light can provide spatiotemporal control over synthetic cell functions relevant to future therapeutic applications. We compare external control modalities and review optical strategies that regulate synthetic cell functions across multiple functional layers, including biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport and release, communication, and systems-level integration. Particular emphasis is placed on integrating optical control with cell-free expression systems, RNA-based regulatory platforms, membrane engineering, and emerging synthetic cell architectures. We further discuss challenges associated with system integration, biomolecule complexity, energy management, light delivery, and translation. By classifying optical methodologies according to the functional layers they regulate, we provide a methodology-centered framework for comparing and integrating optical-control strategies toward increasingly sophisticated light-responsive synthetic cell platforms for future therapeutic applications.

item.title: Synthetic Biology Toolbox for Lactiplantibacillus plantarum: Engineering Next-Generation Probiotic Cell Factories.
item.abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum has emerged as a promising synthetic biology chassis owing to its food-grade safety, probiotic properties, and adaptability to the gastrointestinal tract. Its engineering potential has expanded rapidly in live biotherapeutics, functional foods, biosensors, and animal health. However, its broader application is still limited by the lack of standardized genetic parts, versatile engineering tools, and industrially compatible chassis. This review summarizes recent advances in the synthetic biology toolbox of L. plantarum, including expression elements, genome engineering strategies, and representative applications. Particular emphasis is placed on the development of genetic components, conventional and CRISPR-based engineering technologies, and their applications in medicine, food biotechnology, biosensing, and animal nutrition. Current challenges and future opportunities, including standardized genetic parts, precision genome engineering, AI-assisted strain design, and high-performance chassis development, are also discussed. This review provides a comprehensive framework for developing next-generation programmable probiotic cell factories based on L. plantarum.

item.title: Quorum-Sensing-Mediated Extracellular Electron Transfer Enables Hydrogel Morphogenesis.
item.abstract: Engineered living materials seek to capture the sensitivity, responsiveness, and programmable characteristics of biological systems. One emergent property of living systems is genetically driven spatial patterning, which controls cell differentiation and the development of complex multicellular organisms. Inspired by this capability, we use bacteria to spatially control material assembly. In our system, extracellular electron transfer (EET) flux from Shewanella oneidensis drives hydrogel synthesis via copper-catalyzed radical polymerization. We first construct a recombinant quorum-sensing system in S. oneidensis that allows for cell-cell communication between "sender" and "receiver" cells through an autoinducer. We then examine controlled gene expression and EET-driven chemical transformation in various synthetic consortia. Via diffusion through agarose, we examine 2D patterns of gene expression relative to localized sender cell populations and demonstrate controlled hydrogel crosslinking in predictable patterns. Finally, we apply computational methods and NOT logic in "receiver" cells toward more complex patterns of gene expression. Our results highlight the potential of bacteria to program material systems with life-like properties, including self-assembly, environmental responsiveness, and patterned differentiation.
item.authors: Miniel Mahfoud, Damani, Partipilo, et al.

item.title: Engineering a hemoglobin variant with enhanced stability and oxygen affinity using a protein language model.
item.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Engineered hemoglobin variants offer therapeutic promise for artificial blood substitutes and oxygen therapeutics, but rational design is constrained by protein stability and heme-binding. Protein language models (pLMs) predict mutation fitness, yet their integration with biophysical validation remains limited.
METHODS: We developed a hybrid pipeline combining pLM (ESM3) with molecular docking, Monte Carlo simulation, molecular dynamics, MM-GBSA/PBSA binding free energy calculations, and density functional theory (DFT) to engineer a stabilized hemoglobin variant (esmHb) with enhanced oxygen affinity, benchmarking against the clinically characterized Hb Fort de France mutation (α45 His→Arg).
RESULTS: ESM3 accurately assessed the fitness effect of the Hb Fort de France mutation and generated structurally stable esmHb models. Compared with the wild-type variant (wtHb), esmHb exhibited improved thermodynamic stability (ΔG: -18.48 vs. -12.22 kcal/mol), increased heme-binding affinity (ΔGbind: -11.79 vs. -8.42 kcal/mol), and greater thermodynamic favorability of oxidation according to DFT calculations (ΔE: -173.1 vs. -149.9 kcal/mol). MM-GBSA and MM-PBSA binding free energy calculations further supported improved protein-heme and protein-protein interactions, with esmHb showing more favorable values in both implicit solvation models. Statistical significance (p < 0.05) was reached for protein-protein interactions via both methods and for protein-heme interactions via MM-PBSA. We interpret the MM-GBSA results as a suggestive trend rather than definitive evidence.
DISCUSSION: This work establishes a generalizable framework for pLM-driven protein engineering applicable to therapeutic Hb variants and beyond.

item.title: RNA-Based Biosensors in Microbial Cell Factory Engineering: A Hierarchical Framework From Enzyme to Host-Level Engineering.
item.abstract: Microbial cell factory development requires iterative optimization of enzymes, pathway fluxes, and cell traits to achieve efficient and robust production of target chemicals. However, the complexity of intracellular metabolic networks often limits predictable identification and control of engineering targets. Genetically encoded metabolite-responsive RNA biosensors based on aptamer recognition and riboswitch- or ribozyme-mediated regulation have emerged as versatile tools for linking intracellular metabolite levels to measurable or selectable outputs. Their rapid signal transduction, compact genetic architecture, and low metabolic burden make them attractive for high-throughput screening and dynamic regulation. This Review adopts a hierarchical engineering framework that examines RNA biosensor applications across progressively broader levels, from enzyme engineering to pathway-level regulation and host-level cellular trait engineering. We further discuss their molecular organization and technological evolution, including ligand recognition, regulatory coupling, sensor tuning, and computational approaches. Finally, challenges associated with sensor robustness, host dependency, scalability, and translation into production-relevant phenotypes are discussed together with opportunities in cell-free characterization and data-driven design. This hierarchical perspective highlights RNA biosensors as engineering interfaces connecting intracellular sensing with interventions across multiple scales of microbial cell factory engineering.

item.title: From genome editing to chromosome engineering in plants.
item.abstract: Engineering large genomic segments is rapidly expanding the scope of plant genome manipulation from individual genes to chromosome-scale redesign. Recent advances in double-strand break-, prime-editing-, recombinase-, and transposase-based technologies now enable programmable deletion, insertion, replacement, duplication, inversion, and translocation of DNA fragments ranging from kilobases to megabases. In this review, we summarize the major strategies for large-fragment genome engineering in plants, compare their strengths and limitations, and discuss their applications in both fundamental plant biology and crop breeding. We further highlight that the integration of artificial intelligence is catalyzing the rapid optimization of large-fragment genome engineering. The ongoing transition from genome editing to chromosome engineering promises to revolutionize crop breeding and plant synthetic biology, ultimately enabling rational design of plant genomes.

item.title: Genome editing beyond transgenes: DNA-free technologies in crop improvement.
item.abstract: Conventional and transgenic approaches to crop improvement are increasingly constrained by biosafety concerns, stringent regulatory frameworks, and limited public acceptance, necessitating new precision breeding methods. DNA-free genome editing using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach has emerged as a transformative approach that enables precise, targeted genetic modifications without the stable integration of a foreign gene (transgene). This strategy transiently introduces CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, or in vitro transcribed mRNA, into plant cells. This review focuses primarily on CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing and its applications in crop improvement. After targeted genome cleavage, the editing elements are rapidly degraded, leaving only the desired genomic modification and resulting in plants indistinguishable from those developed through conventional breeding. To achieve targeted, DNA-free genome editing, researchers have developed numerous molecular platforms and delivery systems, such as protoplast transfection, biolistic bombardment, nanoparticle-based systems, and emerging pollen- and meristem-targeted systems, for major crop species. Researchers have successfully enhanced several notable traits, including disease and pest resistance, nutritional quality, abiotic stress tolerance, and agronomic performance, in cereals, vegetables, oilseeds, and perennial crops. Recent advancements, including base editing, prime editing, and multiplex gene editing, are further expanding the precision, efficiency, and scope of DNA-free genome editing. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing offers a route to crop improvement that avoids stable transgene integration, though its wider deployment depends on progress in regeneration, molecular validation, and regulatory convergence.

item.title: Enhanced Fidelity and Sequence Generality of an RNA Polymerase Ribozyme
item.abstract: Directed evolution has been used to develop RNA enzymes (ribozymes) that catalyze the RNA-templated polymerization of RNA. The more advanced polymerases can synthesize long RNA products, but have shortcomings with regard to copying accuracy and template sequence generality, which are impediments to using the polymerase to replicate and evolve other functional RNAs. By applying stringent selection pressure over the course of 33 successive rounds of evolution, both the fidelity and sequence generality of the polymerase were greatly improved. When synthesizing large functional RNAs such as the class I ligase ribozyme, the fidelity improved from 86% to 94% per nucleotide, due to both reduced incorporation of mismatched nucleotides and reduced propensity to extend partial-length products that have mismatched termini. The improved polymerase is also able to synthesize a broad range of RNA products, including those that require copying templates that are highly structured or contain sequences that previously were difficult to copy.
item.authors: Horning, D. P.,  Nasser, S. C.,  Joyce, G. F.

item.title: Artificial photosynthetic cells: bridging chemical energization with biological functionalization.
item.abstract: Artificial photosynthetic cells are nature-inspired systems that reproduce photosynthetic functions within cell/cell-mimetic compartments. Unlike discrete photocatalytic platforms, they integrate light harvesting, charge separation, multistep catalysis, selective transport, and compartmentalization to convert isolated photochemical reactions into coordinated cell-like functions. Driven by needs in carbon-neutral manufacturing, sustainable solar conversion, and precision medicine, the field is advancing from simple photocatalytic vesicles toward integrated and increasingly synthetic-cell platforms. In this review, we systematically elaborate on the rational design principles and emergent functional landscapes of artificial photosynthetic cells from a bioinspired perspective. We first decode the fundamental operational logic of natural photosynthesis, serving as a design blueprint. We then summarize the core construction modules of artificial photosynthetic cells, including cell-mimetic chassis, high-performance light-harvesting engines, multi-level catalytic networks, and precise interfacial engineering strategies. Furthermore, we categorize assembly paradigms into three mainstream branches: semi-artificial biohybrid systems, bottom-up reconstituted synthetic systems, and fully abiotic photosynthetic mimics. We further highlight a series of current and prospective functionalities, ranging from solar-driven CO2 fixation and high-value chemical synthesis to in situ biomedical drug generation, as well as primitive life-like characteristics including intercellular communication, motility, and compartment division. Finally, we pinpoint the key technical bottlenecks, common pitfalls and outline opportunities enabled by the deep integration of synthetic biology, functional materials chemistry, and systematic bioengineering.

item.title: A base-editing and auxotrophic selection platform for linking epigenetic regulators to silent biosynthetic gene clusters in Aspergillus nidulans.
item.abstract: Filamentous fungi harbor numerous silent biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), representing an underexplored reservoir of natural products. Chemical inhibition of epigenetic regulators is an effective strategy for activating silent BGCs, but it often lacks specificity and cannot readily link activated clusters to their cognate regulators. Here, we developed a coupled cytosine base editing and auxotrophic selection platform in Aspergillus nidulans to systematically identify epigenetic regulators of silent gene clusters. An sgRNA library targeting 24 core epigenetic regulators was introduced, together with a cytosine base editor, into 21 pyrG-based PKS reporter strains, enabling growth-based selection and direct sgRNA recovery by Sanger sequencing. This screen identified five regulator-cluster activation pairs, including known interactions and two previously uncharacterized mechanisms. Specifically, KdmB represses the AN7084 gene cluster by erasing promoter H3K4me3, whereas Kmt5 silences the cichorine core pks gene through H4K20me3 deposition. This scalable platform enables rapid matching of silent BGCs with their epigenetic regulators and advances chromatin-guided fungal genome mining.

item.title: Editing Enzymes with Multiscale Metal-Based Components.
item.abstract: Enzymes are powerful natural catalysts distinguished by high efficiency and selectivity. The use of enzymes in the chemical industry can theoretically enable numerous efficient and sustainable reaction pathways. Nevertheless, the application of enzymes is hindered by their narrow catalytic repertoire. Enzymes are readily deactivated under nonnatural environments, and their reaction types are limited. Developing enzymes with new catalytic functions has been a longstanding challenge in the field of biocatalysis. Strategies such as directed evolution and de novo protein design have been very successful in designing new enzymes. However, as both approaches rely on the engineering of amino acid sequences of proteins, they remain constrained and cannot fully meet the growing demand for non-natural biocatalysis. Incorporating abiotic components with enzymes is a powerful tool for editing enzymes to render new catalytic capabilities. Metal-based components possess a broad catalytic repertoire, structural stability, and multifunctionality, making them promising building blocks for enzyme editing. This Account summarizes our contributions over the past decade in editing enzyme catalysts with metal-based components as a scale-dependent evolution, from nanoscale environmental modulation to atom-scale active site redefinition, illustrating how enzyme editing with metal-based components can systematically address non-natural catalytic challenges. A conceptual framework in which enzymes are edited with metal-based components across scales from the nanometer to the atomic dimension is introduced, establishing a logical basis for integrating biocatalysis with abiotic reactivity. At the nanoscale, enzymes are encapsulated in metal-based frameworks to improve the configuration stability, enabling catalysis under non-native and harsh conditions. The robustness of enzymes under extreme pH, high temperature, and organic solvent can be largely enhanced through the regulation of metal-based frameworks. At the sub-nanoscale, metal clusters are embedded within enzyme scaffolds to construct enzyme-metal hybrid catalysts. By integration of enzymatic and chemical catalysis, new non-natural catalytic processes can be established. At the atomic scale, metal atoms are incorporated into the enzyme catalytic pocket, creating new hybrid active sites. The hybrid active site endows an enzyme with capabilities to drive new-to-nature reactions, unlocking an expanded enzyme catalytic space. This work provides a unifying conceptual framework that clarifies how metal-based components can be strategically employed to reprogram enzyme stability, functionality, and reactivity. We hope that the strategies and concepts discussed herein offer comprehensive design principles for biohybrid catalysts and establish a foundation for reprogramming enzymatic function beyond evolutionary limitations.

item.title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
item.abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biologics, a comprehensive understanding of how these innovations intersect with precision medicine remains limited. This review addresses this gap by summarizing the major contemporary approaches used in therapeutic protein engineering, including directed evolution, rational design, and de novo protein design, and by analyzing their roles in enabling patient-tailored interventions. It provides an integrated overview of the clinical applications of engineered therapeutic proteins across key medical fields, supported by a list of U.S. Food and Drug Administration- and European Medicines Agency-approved protein therapeutics from 2020 to 2025. The review further provides a comparative perspective on major protein engineering strategies, highlighting their relative advantages and limitations, while examining differences in clinical translation across major disease areas. By combining technological advances with disease-specific applications, this review offers a perspective that has not been fully developed in the literature. Finally, the review discusses the current challenges affecting the implementation of precision medicine, including immunogenicity, regulatory constraints, and ethical considerations, and outlines future directions, such as artificial intelligence-guided protein design, targeted protein degradation, and personalized vaccine development. Collectively, these insights highlight the expanding role of engineered proteins in shaping the next-generation of precision therapeutics and emphasize the growing importance of integrating multidisciplinary approaches to advance therapeutic innovation in modern clinical practice.

item.title: Expanding photosynthesis through biosolar oxic N2 fixation: toward a sustainable BioNitrogen Economy.
item.abstract: Atmospheric dinitrogen (N2) is far more abundant than carbon dioxide (CO2), yet photosynthesis has been studied and harnessed predominantly for photosynthetic carbon fixation (PCF), underpinning the global biocarbon economy. In contrast, biological N2 fixation-the natural gateway for atmospheric nitrogen into the biosphere-remains comparatively underexploited. Modern agriculture and industry consequently depend heavily on the fossil-fuel-intensive Haber-Bosch process, with substantial energy and environmental costs. Diazotrophic cyanobacteria offer a fundamentally different paradigm by coupling oxygenic photosynthesis to nitrogenase-mediated N2 fixation. We term this process photosynthetic nitrogen fixation (PNF), which uses solar energy to convert water and atmospheric N2 into bioavailable nitrogen. Beyond its ecological significance, PNF expands the functional scope of photosynthesis beyond carbon fixation and provides a biological foundation for sustainable nitrogen production, biofertilization, and N2-based biosolar manufacturing. Recent advances in cyanobacterial physiology, ecology, evolution, synthetic biology, and AI-enabled multi-omics are accelerating efforts to harness this potential. This review examines the diversity of diazotrophic cyanobacteria, their strategies for protecting oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase, and emerging approaches for genetic engineering cyanobacteria as programmable platforms for nitrogen production and crop-associated nitrogen delivery. We further propose a roadmap toward a solar-powered BioNitrogen Economy encompassing bioprospecting, synthetic biology, genomic engineering, crop integration, and scalable agricultural and industrial deployment. By expanding photosynthesis from carbon fixation to the solar-powered capture of both carbon and atmospheric nitrogen, PNF could help drive the transition from a fossil-fuel-dependent chemo-nitrogen economy toward a sustainable BioNitrogen Civilization.

item.title: Engineering organoids toward implantable living therapeutics.
item.abstract: Stem cell-derived organoids are emerging as living therapeutics for repairing or replacing damaged tissues and organs, offering new opportunities for regenerative medicine. However, their clinical translation remains limited by immune rejection, insufficient functional integration, and low manufacturing throughput. In this review, we summarize recent advances in engineering organoids toward implantable living therapeutics by examining how hydrogel engineering, microfluidic chips, three-dimensional bioprinting, and synthetic biology overcome key translational barriers and facilitate the in vivo application of organoids. We further discuss the existing regulatory frameworks supporting the clinical translation of organoid-based therapies. Current evidence indicates that these bioengineering strategies enhance graft survival, tissue integration, and therapeutic efficacy through complementary mechanisms, including immunomodulatory signals, biomimetic microenvironments, hierarchical tissue architectures, and programmable cellular functions. Importantly, engineered organoids have been successfully applied to restore hair-bearing skin, repair colonic epithelial continuity, bridge critical-size bone defects, and correct metabolic disorders. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in quality-control standardization, scalable manufacturing, regulatory harmonization, and long-term safety assessment. Future studies integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and intelligent living devices are warranted to facilitate high-fidelity manufacturing, quality inspection, real-time monitoring, and closed-loop therapeutic regulation in clinical practice. Collectively, engineered organoids represent a promising frontier for new-generation transplantation and regenerative medicine.

item.title: Additive Manufacturing of Metabolically Active Living Materials with Enhanced Biocontainment.
item.abstract: Additive manufacturing of engineered living materials (ELMs) enables the spatial patterning of living cells or organisms within three-dimensional (3D) polymer matrices. However, effective biocontainment, defined as the ability to retain cells within 3D-printed matrices during the application period, remains a key limitation for ELMs requiring physical confinement. While synthetic biology provides cell-specific biocontainment strategies, materials-based approaches can enable generic cell retention capabilities. Therefore, we applied a materials-based strategy that combines pre-printing formulation development and post-printing processing to increase the retention of yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae in Pluronic F127-bisurethane methacrylate (F127-BUM) hydrogels. F127-BUM precursor solutions were formulated with the comonomers methacrylic acid (MAA) and/or 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl methacrylate (DMAEMA), extrusion-printed, UV-cross-linked, and immersed in 70 vol % ethanol for 60 or 300 s before cultivation. Comonomer addition preserved dimensional fidelity, thermoresponsiveness, and shear-thinning behavior for 3D printing. After immobilization and cross-linking, DMAEMA and higher concentrations of MAA considerably reduced yeast viability, whereas a 70-80% viability was observed for 0.03 and 0.06 mol L-1 MAA. With 0.06 mol L-1 MAA and 300 s ethanol immersion, the yeast retention time reached 98 ± 12 h, which was approximately 48% longer than that of the correspondingly treated F127-BUM-only control and represented about a 465% increase relative to the untreated F127-BUM-only control. After ethanol immersion, a peripheral growth-free zone developed around a metabolically active core, enhancing cell retention and contributing to delayed cell escape. The selected MAA-containing ELMs remained metabolically active and showed nearly 38% higher apparent glucose-to-ethanol conversion than treated F127-BUM-only controls. The suspension cultures fermented faster and achieved higher yield. Our method achieved enhanced biocontainment, with an operational window of about 4-5 days. In conclusion, we demonstrate that combining pre-printing and post-printing processes can enhance biocontainment for different ELM applications. We suggest the integration of this method with synthetic-biology strategies to further extend biocontainment duration for metabolically active living materials.

item.title: Comparative analysis of precursor supply and pathway reinforcement strategies for shikimic acid biosynthesis in Pseudomonas putida.
item.abstract: The shikimate pathway is a central metabolic route for the biosynthesis of high-value aromatic compounds. Traditional metabolic engineering strategies have largely focused on overexpressing pathway-specific genes, enhancing precursor supply, or introducing feedback-resistant variants of 3-deoxy-D-arabino-heptulosonate 7-phosphate (DAHP) synthase to increase pathway flux. However, how these distinct strategies differentially affect flux distribution and the accumulation of key intermediates, specifically 3-dehydroshikimate (DHS) and shikimic acid (SA), remains largely unexplored in Pseudomonas putida (P. putida). Here, we systematically assess the effects of commonly applied engineering strategies on DHS and SA production using distinct SA pathway modules. The results show that overexpression of transketolase I (tktA), phosphoenolpyruvate synthase (ppsA), and SA pathway genes (aroE, aroB, aroQ-II), together with heterologous expression of feedback-resistant aroG, in a genome-edited P. putida EM42 strain harboring pykA/pykF deletions and a hexR knockout, yielded approximately 71 mg L⁻1 shikimic acid, corresponding to a > 284-fold increase relative to the wild-type EM42. Notably, the findings reveal that following the relief of precursor constraints, the achievable maximum titer is unaffected by the particular DAHP synthase isoform utilized. Furthermore, the standalone overexpression of ppsA and tktA yielded SA and DHS levels comparable to those achieved with the additional expression of the aforementioned pathway genes. However, despite this phenotypic convergence in titers, comparative transcriptomic analysis revealed that the genetic route taken to reach these levels is associated with markedly distinct transcriptional configurations of the host metabolic network. In the same genetic background, amplification of ppsA-tktA alone is associated with an increased transcriptional investment in the biosynthesis of essential cofactors and metabolic precursors, whereas overexpression of the SA pathway is accompanied by enrichment of protocatechuate catabolic genes, consistent with the intrinsic aromatic funneling capacity of P. putida under conditions of elevated shikimate pathway flux. These results demonstrate that evaluating engineering success solely based on final product yields obscures substantial differences in underlying metabolic states. Accordingly, we propose that tailored engineering strategies guided by key pathway intermediates are critical for the rational optimization of P. putida as an efficient cell factory.

item.title: APR-Score: Identification and Scoring of Aggregation-prone Regions in Protein Sequences.
item.abstract: Protein aggregation is a critical phenomenon associated with numerous neurodegenerative and systemic diseases. Understanding the propensity of proteins to aggregate is essential for unraveling the molecular basis of these disorders and for the design and engineering of novel proteins, as well as for modulating the activity/stability of enzymatic proteins. Here, we present APR-Score, a novel machine learning-based computational method designed to identify aggregation-prone regions within protein sequences. APR-Score leverages a combination of sequence-based features to predict regions of proteins that are prone to aggregation. It harnessed the information embedded in compiled sequence and structural features to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. The method was evaluated through rigorous cross-validation on the training dataset and further validated on an independent test dataset. APR-Score demonstrated robustness and reliability in distinguishing aggregation-prone regions from non-aggregating ones, achieving a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.77, precision of 0.89, and F1-Score of 0.87. This tool offers significant value for researchers investigating protein aggregation-related diseases, as it can expedite the identification of aggregation-prone regions, thereby aiding the development of targeted therapies and diagnostic tools. Moreover, computational protein design and engineering efforts can be facilitated by APR-Score-based identification and screening of aggregation-prone protein sequences. APR-Score is available at https://github.com/TII-BRC/APR-Score.
